title: Supervision 3 essay
description: How are movements on the cellular and molecular scale used to produce movement of whole animals?
instructions:
This is the work to hand in for Supervision 3. Write it here in one sitting, the same way you’ll write your essays in the online exam.

  • Time. There’s no time limit, but give yourself about 40 minutes. The clock at the top counts the time you spend writing and tells you when you reach 40 minutes. Spend the first few minutes planning, on paper if you like.
  • Pasting. As in the exam, you can copy and paste within your essay, but you can’t paste in text copied from anywhere else. Write everything in your own words.
  • Diagrams. You can add diagrams, just as you can in the exam. Draw one with Insert drawing (the pencil), or use Insert picture to add a picture, such as a photo of a diagram you drew on paper. Type a caption under it. Your pictures go into the Word document with your essay.
  • Saving. Your essay is saved in this browser as you type, so you can leave and come back to it.
  • When you’ve finished, go to the submission page (the last tile at the bottom), check your essay and submit it. Then hand it in as described below.

questions.title: Movement, from molecules to whole animals
questions.text:
How are movements on the cellular and molecular scale used to produce movement of whole animals?

Write in continuous prose, with an introduction, paragraphs that each make one point, and a conclusion. Use specific examples and numbers from the lectures, and explain how each one helps to answer the question.
questions.guidance:
Read this after you’ve written your essay, and use it to look back over what you wrote before the supervision. It isn’t a model essay. It sets out the ground a good answer covers, and the questions it should ask.

What the title asks. “How” asks for mechanisms, explained step by step, and “used to produce” asks you to connect the scales. A myosin head moves an actin filament about 10 nm, and an animal moves metres, so the heart of a good answer is how those tiny movements are added up, switched on together, controlled and passed on to the skeleton. An essay that describes each scale well but never says how one produces the next misses the point of the title.

  • The molecular motor. Myosin II turns the chemical energy of ATP into mechanical work in the cross-bridge cycle. ATP binding detaches the head from actin, and its hydrolysis cocks the head. The cocked head binds actin again, and the release of Pi triggers the power stroke, which moves the actin filament by about 10 nm. ADP is released, leaving the head tightly bound in the rigor state until the next ATP arrives, which is why muscles stiffen in rigor mortis, when ATP runs out. Each cycle uses one ATP. Myosin moves towards the plus ends of the actin filaments, which are anchored at the Z discs, so the two halves of each bipolar thick filament pull the thin filaments towards the middle of the sarcomere.
  • From molecules to sarcomeres. In the sliding filament theory (A. F. Huxley and Niedergerke, and H. E. Huxley and Hanson, both in 1954), the filaments slide past each other without changing length, so the I band and the H zone narrow while the A band stays the same. Each thick filament has about 300 myosin molecules, whose heads cycle out of step with each other, so that some are always attached and the filament doesn’t slip back. Structural proteins keep everything in register: α-actinin at the Z disc, titin (a molecular spring that holds the thick filament in the middle of the sarcomere and gives passive tension) and nebulin along the thin filaments.
  • Adding up, in series and in parallel. Thousands of sarcomeres lie end to end in each myofibril, so their shortening and their velocities add, and a muscle’s maximum velocity is proportional to its length. Myofibrils and fibres lie side by side, so their forces add, and a muscle’s maximum force is proportional to the number of thick filaments in its cross-section. That explains the shapes of muscles: long, parallel-fibred strap muscles give range and speed, and pennate muscles pack in more fibres for force.
  • Switching it on together. Excitation–contraction coupling starts millions of motors across a fibre within milliseconds of each other. The motor neuron’s action potential releases acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, and the muscle action potential spreads along the sarcolemma and down the T-tubules. There, dihydropyridine receptors (L-type Ca2+ channels acting as voltage sensors) are coupled mechanically to ryanodine receptors in the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which release Ca2+. Ca2+ binds troponin C, tropomyosin moves, and the myosin-binding sites on actin are exposed. SERCA pumps take the Ca2+ back up, using ATP (calsequestrin stores it), and the muscle relaxes. Fibres are up to 100 µm across, and diffusion from the surface would be far too slow and uneven, which is why the T-tubules matter.
  • Controlling the force. A single action potential gives a twitch, which lasts much longer than the action potential itself, so repeated stimuli summate and, at high enough frequencies, fuse into a tetanus. The nervous system grades force by how fast it fires and by how many motor units it recruits, small, slow ones first and large, fast ones later (the size principle). Force also depends on length, because the length–tension relationship follows the overlap of the filaments, and on velocity.
  • Force, velocity and power. The heavier the load, the more slowly a muscle shortens, because more cross-bridges must be attached at once to bear it (Hill, 1938). Power, force × velocity, is greatest at about a third of the maximum force and velocity. A muscle that is stretched while it’s active (an eccentric contraction) resists with more force than it can exert isometrically.
  • From muscle to limb. Tendons pass the force on to bones, which act as levers about the joints. Most muscles pull close to the joint (the biceps about 4 cm from the elbow, with the hand about 35 cm away), so they work at a disadvantage in force but move the limb much further and faster than they shorten. Different animals are geared for different jobs: diggers such as armadillos for force, runners such as horses for speed. Tendons are springs too, storing elastic energy and giving it back at each stride, as in a hopping kangaroo, or in a running person’s Achilles tendon.
  • Matching muscles to tasks. Fibre types differ in speed, metabolism and fatigue: type I (slow, oxidative), IIa (fast, oxidative) and IIb (fast, glycolytic). The soleus, a postural muscle, is mostly type I, while the gastrocnemius, used for jumping and sprinting, has many more fast fibres. ATP is supplied by creatine phosphate for the first few seconds, and then by glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation.
  • Evaluation and breadth. You could ask whether all animals move like this. Smooth muscle uses the same actin and myosin, regulated differently (through phosphorylation of the myosin light chain), for slow, sustained contractions inside the body rather than for moving the animal. An earthworm’s muscles push against a hydrostatic skeleton of fluid, and an octopus’s arm is a muscular hydrostat, with no skeleton at all. Many small animals, such as comb jellies, flatworms and many marine larvae, swim or glide by beating cilia, which are driven by a different motor protein, dynein. Diseases show that every link in the chain matters: myasthenia gravis at the neuromuscular junction, malignant hyperthermia at the ryanodine receptor, and Duchenne muscular dystrophy in the link between the cytoskeleton and the membrane.

Against the core criteria. Does each paragraph move up a scale and say how the scale below produces it? Do you take a position early on? You might argue, for example, that the movement of a whole animal comes from vast numbers of identical molecular steps, added up in series and in parallel, switched on together, graded by the nervous system and geared by the skeleton. Do you use specific numbers and examples, rather than general statements? Does the conclusion pull the scales together?
